channel_name: This Week in Startups · Jason Calacanis
video_title: Dario Predicts the End of Cancer, Will AI Replace VCs & the SPV Fee Trap
gist: A VC roundtable (Jason Calacanis, DA Wallach of Time BioVentures, Jenny Fielding of Everywhere Ventures, Ben Lerer of Lerer Hippeau) on how AI is changing venture work, why cheap vibe-coded software shrinks moats and pushes pricing toward pay-for-work, how family offices are moving money from funds into SPVs while emerging-manager fundraising collapses and SPV fee structures get abusive, and why the panel puts low odds (0-5%) on Dario Amodei's claim that cancer, Alzheimer's and mental illness will be gone within a decade.

insights.claim: Founders are starting to send VCs company.md markdown files built for investors to load into an LLM and question, instead of (or alongside) pitch decks and calls.
insights.speaker: DA Wallach
insights.so_what: Startup discovery and diligence are becoming agent-mediated, so the useful signal moves to what holds up under machine Q&A rather than how polished the deck is.

insights.claim: Everywhere Ventures found that about 99% of VC firm websites it reviewed were not optimized for AI agents (no FAQs or agent-readable pages), and after optimizing its own site it saw itself surfaced more in agent results as a pre-seed fund.
insights.speaker: Jenny Fielding
insights.so_what: Being optimized for agent search (generative-engine optimization) is an early, cheap distribution edge for small funds and startups.
insights.quote: 99% of the websites that we looked at of other VC firms weren't optimized for um the agentic world

insights.claim: Lerer Hippeau finds AI deal analysis and market mapping high quality, but its investment recommendations are consistently low-conviction: on a 1-9 scale with no 5s, AI scores deals 3, 4, 6 or 7 almost every time.
insights.speaker: Ben Lerer
insights.so_what: LLMs can't yet make the decisive, outlier calls venture returns depend on, so human conviction is still where a fund's edge comes from.
insights.quote: we get scores between three, four, six, and seven almost 100% of the time, which is just like a pretty weakwilled

insights.claim: Lerer Hippeau runs multiple AI agents that score founders on domain expertise and on how they handle being challenged, then feeds those scores into a fund model trained on where past fund-returners came from, to test whether the ownership math works.
insights.speaker: Ben Lerer
insights.so_what: Firm-built scoring plus portfolio-construction models are becoming standard VC tooling, and a deal now has to clear both a quality bar and an ownership bar.

insights.claim: Josh Wolfe has said Lux Capital's biggest successes were deals the partners fought over, which suggests today's late-stage vintage is risky because the capital is going to highly consensus companies.
insights.speaker: DA Wallach / Ben Lerer
insights.so_what: Be wary of late-stage vintages where every deal looks obvious, because consensus deals have historically underperformed.
insights.quote: we should be concerned about this vintage for latestage companies

insights.claim: DA Wallach argues it is inconsistent to believe AI will solve hard problems in science and finance but cannot rigorously evaluate startups, which calls into question whether VC analyst jobs survive the next 6-12 months.
insights.speaker: DA Wallach
insights.so_what: Expect the analytical part of venture to be automated, with VC value shifting to relationships, access and judgment.
insights.quote: why do you believe that we should have jobs past 6 months from now or a year from now?

insights.claim: Jenny Fielding says venture capitalist will not be a profession of the future, though the human roles of coach, cheerleader and confidant to founders will remain.
insights.speaker: Jenny Fielding
insights.so_what: The VC role will narrow toward founder support, with picking increasingly done by algorithms.
insights.quote: I don't think venture capitalists are a profession of the future.

insights.claim: Ben Lerer accepts that algorithms may pick better than VCs, but argues AI cannot build trust or be a founder's 'first call on the worst day', and he uses AI to automate everything else so partners can spend more time with founders.
insights.speaker: Ben Lerer
insights.so_what: Durable advantage for VC firms moves to relationship capacity, with AI acting as leverage rather than a replacement.
insights.quote: I want to be your first call on your worst day. And I don't think that AI is ever going to replace that.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis has been pitched a startup where a well-known VC firm vibe coded the product in-house and made one of its own GPs the founder, which he calls the first VC-as-founder case he has seen.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: VC firms that build startups themselves will compete with independent founders and change incubation economics.

themes.theme: Pre-seed picking, pivots and ownership math

insights.claim: At pre-seed, roughly a third to half of portfolio companies pivot significantly, and many of the biggest winners are among them, so first-check investors are mostly betting on founders.
insights.speaker: Jenny Fielding / Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Pre-seed underwriting should weight the founder over the initial idea.
insights.quote: I'd say in our portfolio at least a third and some of our biggest companies have pivoted.

insights.claim: Ben Lerer expects more startup pivots now because foundation models keep moving into new areas, so it's unclear which business models and moats will last; software can pivot quickly (Cursor is an example), while hardware and biotech pivots are costly.
insights.speaker: Ben Lerer
insights.so_what: Software startups can pivot cheaply, which favors flexible early bets on founders over thesis-locked bets.
insights.quote: it's just not clear what the enduring models and moes are going to be

insights.claim: Biotech startups rarely pivot after picking an indication, because the fixed costs of clinical trials lock them in through at least the first human trial; exploration happens before that point.
insights.speaker: DA Wallach
insights.so_what: In biotech, choosing the indication is the key underwriting decision because it is close to irreversible.

insights.claim: Micro One, LAUNCH Fund 4's best-returning investment, started as AI vetting of top developers, pivoted to selling data to LLM labs, and now has about $1B in revenue; LAUNCH invested at a $12M valuation.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Supplying training data to AI labs has produced outsized revenue, and founder-led pivots toward that demand can return a whole fund.
insights.quote: they're at a billion dollars in revenue right now.

insights.claim: Lerer Hippeau backed Zipline when it made toy robots for kids, before it became a fixed-wing drone blood-delivery company in Africa, which shows the value of backing exceptional founders before the idea is clear.
insights.speaker: Ben Lerer
insights.so_what: Some of the largest venture outcomes look un-investable at the first check.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis passes on small allocations that can't return a fund: for example, $100K at a $20M valuation from a $45M fund is about 50 basis points, which after 50% dilution needs an Uber-sized outcome of about $140B.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Ownership discipline, not deal quality alone, drives fund returns, so token checks waste diligence effort.
insights.quote: Oh, it has to be Uber. It has to be $140 billion.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis says pro-rata rights must be locked in through side letters and defended: he has won 11 of about 12 disputes in which later rounds or founders' lawyers tried to remove early investors' pro-rata.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Early-stage funds increasingly have to enforce their contractual rights to keep access to their winners.

insights.claim: Early-stage investors are favoring younger founders because speed now matters most: moats are smaller, so the advantage goes to teams that are deeply AI-native and run fleets of agents.
insights.speaker: Ben Lerer
insights.so_what: Execution speed is replacing defensibility as the main early-stage selection criterion.
insights.quote: the advantage is that the moes are smaller and so we we favor teams that are going to move faster

themes.theme: Vibe coding, moats and SaaS pricing

insights.claim: Kevin Rose built a Slack alternative in about a month of 4-5 hours a day and released it free on GitHub, while Jack (Square) launched a Slack alternative for developers, showing how cheaply SaaS features can now be copied.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Per-seat SaaS pricing is under pressure from free or near-free copies.

insights.claim: Ben Lerer argues vibe-coded clones don't threaten incumbents without distribution and a data advantage, plus enterprise hardening such as security and SOC 2; he says the 'SaaS apocalypse' hasn't happened yet and calls Slack Salesforce's best acquisition.
insights.speaker: Ben Lerer
insights.so_what: Enterprise SaaS incumbents with distribution and data moats are more durable than the vibe-coding narrative suggests.
insights.quote: the SAS apocalypse of it all hasn't happened yet

insights.claim: Because so many teams can now build the same product, late-stage capital concentrates in companies that appear to have cracked distribution and data moats, such as Instinct at a $30B valuation.
insights.speaker: Ben Lerer
insights.so_what: Commoditized building concentrates late-stage capital in perceived category winners and pushes up their valuations.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis and DA Wallach argue that cheap niche software (for example, $600 per year seats) will force incumbents to rethink pricing, toward flat rates instead of per-seat, because buyers can compare a vendor's price with the cost of building the tool themselves.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis / DA Wallach
insights.so_what: Per-seat SaaS revenue models face compression and resetting market share in vertical niches.
insights.quote: your margins are opportunity

insights.claim: Lerer Hippeau invested in Black Letter, an AI-first law firm that charges for the work rather than the hours, in a category where Crosby moved first.
insights.speaker: Ben Lerer
insights.so_what: Replacing billable hours with fixed fees in professional services is an emerging AI investment category.
insights.quote: It's an AI first law firm where you pay for the work, not for the time.

insights.claim: Everywhere Ventures built Jelly in-house as a cheap PitchBook alternative for emerging managers, adding investor-sentiment signals such as what VCs are saying on Twitter; it drew a 1,000-person beta waitlist and will be priced around $30-50 a month.
insights.speaker: Jenny Fielding
insights.so_what: Expensive data incumbents (PitchBook is about $20K a seat, plus $15K for the API) face vibe-coded niche competitors aimed at underserved small buyers.
insights.quote: pitchbook is about $20,000 a seat. And wow, if you want the API integration, throw in another 15K.

themes.theme: SPVs, LP behavior and the emerging-manager squeeze

insights.claim: Family offices put 34% of their VC commitments into SPVs, up from 9% in 2019, and are choosing individual deals over new 10-year fund commitments.
insights.speaker: Jenny Fielding
insights.so_what: LP capital is moving from blind-pool funds to deal-by-deal exposure, which hurts small fund managers.
insights.quote: family offices put 34% of VC commitments into SPVS um up from 9% in 200 in in 2019.

insights.claim: Ben Lerer says the SPV-share statistic is inflated because OpenAI and Anthropic have absorbed more venture money in four years than any companies in history, much of it through SPVs.
insights.speaker: Ben Lerer
insights.so_what: Read headline venture flow data carefully, since two companies skew the aggregates.

insights.claim: The number of emerging managers closing a fund fell from 927 in 2022 to 448 in 2025, and to 211 in 2026 through Q3; Jenny Fielding expects a large share of that cohort to disappear.
insights.speaker: Jenny Fielding
insights.so_what: Fewer seed funds means less early-stage competition for surviving managers and harder fundraising for new ones.

insights.claim: Ben Lerer predicts sub-$500M funds will raise less this year than in any year in the last decade, with venture split between mega-platforms and early-stage specialists and the middle 'cooked'.
insights.speaker: Ben Lerer
insights.so_what: Mid-sized funds face the worst fundraising squeeze, and the split between early-stage and mega funds will widen.
insights.quote: I believe you will have less money raised by sub$500 million funds this year than in any year in the last decade.

insights.claim: Ben Lerer says LPs that hold four to six mega-platforms are starting to cut some, because the overlapping exposure to the same companies produces average venture returns.
insights.speaker: Ben Lerer
insights.so_what: Mega-fund re-ups may soften as LPs consolidate overlapping exposure.

insights.claim: LAUNCH runs a separate late-stage SPV arm (Vast Space, Travis Kalanick's Atoms, Zipline) with a one-time 2% origination fee and 20% carry; $100M a year of SPV volume yields about $2M to fund the team, and the SPVs bring family offices into its early-stage funds.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Running both funds and SPVs is becoming the standard GP model, with late-stage access serving as the LP acquisition channel.

insights.claim: Some SPV sponsors charge 2-3% fees every year on late-stage positions, which adds up to 15-20% in fees over five years, and Jason Calacanis predicts a wave of SPV lawsuits in the next one to two years.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Check SPV fee structures carefully and expect regulatory or legal scrutiny of opaque SPVs.
insights.quote: The other thing that's going to happen with SPVS, you're going to see this in the next year or two, is a lot of lawsuits.

insights.claim: Jenny Fielding warns that nested SPVs and unclear cap-table positions will lead to disputes and misunderstandings when OpenAI and Anthropic go public.
insights.speaker: Jenny Fielding
insights.so_what: Secondary or SPV holders of AI labs face IPO-time risk over lockups, ownership structure and lack of transparency.

insights.claim: DA Wallach says LPs should benchmark late-stage SPVs (for example, an $8B company's Series C) against public comparables, not early-stage venture funds, because return dispersion, valuations and risk/reward are radically different.
insights.speaker: DA Wallach
insights.so_what: Late-stage private deals should be underwritten like public equities, not as a substitute for venture.
insights.quote: you should be comparing that to public comps

insights.claim: DA Wallach argues incentives align for SPV growth: ex-would-be fund managers become 'freelance investment bankers' who collect fees with no track record, and family-office executives get prestige deals without career risk.
insights.speaker: DA Wallach
insights.so_what: SPV demand is partly driven by status-seeking rather than underwriting, a sign of late-cycle froth in late-stage private markets.
insights.quote: it's cocktail party stuff, but it's not actually perceived as venture risktaking.

insights.claim: Fund managers are increasingly running SPVs into companies that are not in their own portfolios, at LPs' request, which leaves them unable to give an informed recommendation and puts LPs in the position of picking deals.
insights.speaker: Jenny Fielding
insights.so_what: There is now an access-without-information risk in non-portfolio SPVs.
insights.quote: all of a sudden the LPs are becoming pickers.

insights.claim: DA Wallach says strong investor demand for late-stage private AI companies through SPVs shows those companies are ready to go public, and points to a broken IPO market.
insights.speaker: DA Wallach
insights.so_what: Pent-up demand points to a large IPO pipeline once mega private companies list.
insights.quote: tells me those companies are ready to go public.

themes.theme: Dario's 'end of disease' claim and AI hype

insights.claim: Dario Amodei said on the Anthropic roadshow that cancer, Alzheimer's, heart disease and mental illness will be 'relics of the past' in less than a decade.
insights.speaker: Dario Amodei (clip)
insights.so_what: Anthropic's IPO narrative is relying on maximal AI-for-science claims, which buyers should discount.
insights.quote: These will be relics of the past in, I think, less than a decade.

insights.claim: DA Wallach says veteran pharma drug discoverers are skeptical of AI leaders' cure-all promises (such as Demis Hassabis's 'cure all diseases in 10 years') and see them as false hope for patients.
insights.speaker: DA Wallach
insights.so_what: AI drug-discovery timelines promised by tech leaders are likely too short, so price AI-bio assets on realistic clinical timelines.
insights.quote: when Demis says we're going to cure all diseases in 10 years, I think people who have, you know, two PhDs and have been doing this for 40 years go, come on, man.

insights.claim: The panel puts very low odds on Dario's 10-year cure-all scenario: Jason Calacanis says 10 basis points, Ben Lerer says essentially zero, and DA Wallach says 1-5% out of respect for the conviction of leaders like Zuckerberg, Page and Musk.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis / Ben Lerer / DA Wallach
insights.so_what: Experienced investors heavily discount AI utopia scenarios, so valuations that assume them carry downside.
insights.quote: I think my pedario >> pedario >> is between one and five percent.

insights.claim: DA Wallach notes that the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative also promised to cure all disease about 8-10 years ago; it has produced valuable molecular-biology and virtual-cell work but has not cured disease.
insights.speaker: DA Wallach
insights.so_what: A precedent for large AI and biology cure claims falling short of their timelines.

insights.claim: Ben Lerer says the market now demands all-in AI belief ('get in the deepest part of the deep end or get out of the pool'), so that even committed optimists sound like pessimists when they question valuations.
insights.speaker: Ben Lerer
insights.so_what: Herd behavior around AI is a sign of bubble conditions, and Lerer expects some of it to deflate.
insights.quote: get in the deepest part of the deep end or get out of the pool

insights.claim: DA Wallach argues AI leaders, trained as statisticians, should give probabilistic forecasts (for example, '5% chance we cure all diseases in 10 years') instead of binary utopian claims.
insights.speaker: DA Wallach
insights.so_what: Discount AI-lab forecasts that have no probability attached.
insights.quote: these are literally all statisticians who in their public communications have decided to give up on statistics.

themes.theme: Portfolio picks: neurotech, UGC ads, red-teaming

insights.claim: Phantom Neuro (a Time BioVentures seed investment from about three years ago) makes an implant placed under the skin in an amputation stump that reads nerve signals to control a robotic prosthetic; the outpatient procedure takes under an hour, and the first patients were implanted in an Australian study.
insights.speaker: DA Wallach
insights.so_what: A minimally invasive neural interface could reach the large amputee market (including veterans of conflicts like Ukraine) faster than BCI brain implants.

insights.claim: Launchpoint lets brands buy user-generated content (UGC) at scale with Facebook- or TikTok-style targeting, and Ben Lerer calls it the first new scaled performance-marketing channel he has seen since The Trade Desk and AppLovin.
insights.speaker: Ben Lerer
insights.so_what: A new performance ad channel built on the creator economy could take budget from incumbent ad platforms.
insights.quote: It's very rare that you find a real scaled platform to go and do performance marketing and this is the first thing I've seen that looks like that.

insights.claim: LAUNCH-incubated Obliteration.ai offers guardrail-free models (such as GLM) to vetted security teams for red teaming, because frontier models are often restricted for defenders until after attacks happen.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: AI red-teaming tooling for CISOs is an emerging cybersecurity niche.

insights.claim: a16z Speedrun is aggressively competing with Y Combinator: about 10 LAUNCH accelerator companies have gone on to Speedrun, and founders now weigh it against YC.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Mega-platforms are pushing into accelerators, which raises competition for the earliest deals.
